subject: Postdiluvian patriarchal ages (begetting age and remaining years)

figures.name: Shem
figures.note: Begetting age agrees across all three witnesses.

figures.name: Arpachshad
figures.note: LXX and SP add 100 years to the MT begetting age.

figures.name: Cainan (LXX only)
figures.note: LXX inserts an extra patriarch Cainan begetting Shelah at 130; absent in MT and SP.

figures.name: Shelah
figures.note: MT lower by 100 years than LXX/SP.

figures.name: Eber
figures.note: Same +100 pattern in LXX/SP vs MT.

figures.name: Nahor
figures.note: Anomaly: LXX/SP add only 50 years rather than 100.

figures.name: Terah
figures.note: Begetting age of Abram agrees across all witnesses.

systematic_analysis.pattern: For seven of the nine named patriarchs, LXX and SP agree against MT by adding exactly 100 years to the begetting age, with corresponding subtractions from the remainder so total lifespans remain similar. Nahor uniquely receives +50 rather than +100, and the LXX additionally interpolates a second Cainan (130 years) producing a tenfold genealogy mirroring Genesis 5. The pattern is too regular to be coincidental and indicates deliberate redactional activity in at least one tradition.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: In Genesis 11, the Greek and Samaritan versions almost always make each father 100 years older when his son is born than the Hebrew does. The pattern is so consistent that someone clearly altered the numbers on purpose.

theories.name: MT Deflation (Sexton/Green)
theories.summary: Sexton (2018) and Henry Morris/Henry Green argue the LXX/SP preserve the original numbers and the MT systematically subtracted 100 years from each begetting age, possibly to compress chronology so Methuselah dies in the Flood year or to undercut messianic chronological calculations used by Christians. The agreement of LXX and SP against MT is text-critically weighty since they represent independent transmission streams.
theories.summary_plain: Some scholars think the Hebrew text was shortened later, and the Greek and Samaritan versions kept the older, longer numbers. The fact that two independent traditions agree against the Hebrew is strong evidence.
supporting_evidence: LXX and SP agree against MT in seven of nine cases, representing two independent witnesses.
The MT figures make several patriarchs father children before puberty in some reconstructions, while LXX/SP figures are biologically plausible.
Josephus and early Christian chronographers (Africanus, Eusebius) used the longer figures, suggesting they were standard in the Second Temple period.
A deliberate -100 deflation is a simpler editorial act than independent +100 inflations in two traditions.
The MT chronology conveniently makes Shem outlive Abraham, which may reflect later rabbinic harmonization.
weaknesses: No clear theological motive for MT scribes to shorten these specific numbers has been established.
The Nahor anomaly (+50 not +100) is awkward for a clean deflation theory.
Requires positing widespread, coordinated alteration of a sacred text by Masoretic tradents.

theories.name: LXX Inflation
theories.summary: Many scholars (Hendel, Larsson, traditional view) argue that LXX translators or their Hebrew Vorlage inflated begetting ages by 100 to push the Flood and Creation further into the past, aligning biblical chronology with Egyptian/Babylonian antiquity claims and producing a symbolic schema. The SP would then have borrowed or independently developed the same inflation.
theories.summary_plain: Other scholars say the Greek translators added 100 years to make the world seem older, perhaps to compete with Egyptian and Babylonian claims of great antiquity. The Samaritan version may have copied this change.
supporting_evidence: Hellenistic-era apologetic interest in extending biblical antiquity is well-attested in Josephus and Demetrius.
The added Cainan in LXX appears secondary, suggesting LXX expansionism generally.
MT is generally regarded as the more conservative text in numerical matters elsewhere.
A schematic concern to make patriarchs father sons after age 100 (as in Gen 5) explains the +100 rule.
weaknesses: Does not easily explain SP agreement with LXX, since SP is independent of LXX.
No external chronological framework cleanly matches the LXX totals.
The Nahor +50 anomaly is also unexplained on this theory.

theories.name: SP Harmonization
theories.summary: The SP independently harmonized its chronology, possibly under influence of a Hebrew tradition shared with the LXX Vorlage, but is text-critically secondary to the older Hebrew witness. SP's known harmonizing tendencies elsewhere lend some credence, though the Genesis 11 pattern matches LXX too precisely for purely independent harmonization.
theories.summary_plain: The Samaritan Pentateuch is famous for smoothing out the text, so it may have changed the numbers on its own. But the close match with the Greek suggests it isn't acting alone here.
supporting_evidence: SP demonstrably harmonizes elsewhere (e.g., Exodus parallels in Genesis).
SP totals make all patriarchs die before or in the year of Abraham's death, a tidy schema.
SP chronology of Genesis 5 differs from LXX, showing it is not slavishly copying LXX.
weaknesses: Cannot account for LXX's matching figures without invoking a shared Vorlage.
Reduces to either LXX inflation or MT deflation as the underlying explanation.
Does not explain the systematic +100 across both traditions.

theories.name: Theological/Schematic Motivation
theories.summary: The divergences reflect deliberate theological-chronological schemes: MT may compress history to fit a 4000-year Anno Mundi to the Temple/Messiah, while LXX/SP extend it for apologetic or symbolic reasons. The +100 pattern matches Genesis 5's 'fathered after 100' motif, suggesting harmonization between the two genealogies.
theories.summary_plain: The numbers may have been changed for theological reasons, like making world history fit a meaningful total of years. Each tradition shaped the chronology to support its own framework.
supporting_evidence: Rabbinic Seder Olam shows MT chronology serves an Anno Mundi scheme ending circa Bar Kokhba.
LXX chronology yields ~5500 years to Christ, used apologetically by church fathers.
The +100 'father after 100' rule schematically aligns Gen 11 with Gen 5 in LXX/SP.
Numerical symbolism is well-documented in ancient Near Eastern king-lists.
weaknesses: Multiple competing schemes are difficult to verify historically.
Some figures (Nahor, Terah) resist the schematic explanation.
Risks circular reasoning by reading later chronographic systems back into the texts.

theories.name: Scribal Error
theories.summary: Pure accidental scribal error cannot account for a regular +100 differential across nine patriarchs in two independent traditions. Random copying mistakes would produce sporadic, not systematic, divergences.
theories.summary_plain: Simple copying mistakes can't explain the pattern because it's far too regular and consistent.
supporting_evidence: The Nahor anomaly might reflect localized error.
Numerical corruption is common in ancient manuscripts generally.
weaknesses: The +100 regularity is mathematically incompatible with random error.
Two independent traditions making identical errors is statistically negligible.
Cannot account for the inserted Cainan in LXX.

overall_assessment: The Genesis 11 numerical divergences exhibit an unmistakable systematic pattern—LXX and SP agree against MT by +100 years in begetting ages for seven of nine patriarchs—which rules out scribal accident and demands an editorial explanation. The strongest candidates are MT deflation (Sexton, Green) and LXX/SP schematic inflation harmonizing Gen 11 to Gen 5's 'fathered after 100' rule, with theological-chronographic motives plausibly operating in all three streams. The agreement of two independent witnesses (LXX and SP) against MT is text-critically significant and has prompted a recent scholarly reassessment favoring the longer chronology as more original, though the question remains genuinely contested. The episode demonstrates that the Pentateuch's numerical data was an active site of editorial intervention well into the Second Temple period.
overall_plain: The Greek and Samaritan versions consistently make patriarchs 100 years older than the Hebrew when they had children—a pattern too regular to be accidental. Scholars debate whether the Hebrew was shortened or the others lengthened, but recent work increasingly favors the longer numbers as original. Either way, the chronology was clearly edited deliberately by ancient scribes.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Two witnesses against MT: chronology was edited
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The convergent testimony of LXX and SP against MT—two streams that diverge on countless other points—is a rare text-critical phenomenon that reverses the usual presumption favoring MT in numerical matters. Genesis 11 thus becomes a case study in how systematic editorial intervention in sacred numbers persisted into the late Second Temple era, and it suggests the 'original' biblical chronology may be recoverable only through triangulation rather than default deference to the Masoretic tradition.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: When the Greek and Samaritan versions agree against the Hebrew so precisely, it's a serious clue that the Hebrew may have been changed. This forces scholars to weigh all three traditions carefully rather than just trusting one.
